english.title: Arson with intent / reckless as to whether life was endangered
english.standardoffencewording:
On **(..SPECIFY DATE..) at **(..SPECIFY TOWNSHIP..) committed arson in that without lawful excuse

(A)_[destroyed]_
(B)_[damaged]_

by fire **(..SPECIFY THE PROPERTY..)

(C)_[to the value of **(..SPECIFY THE VALUE..)]_
(D)_[of a value unknown]_

belonging to **(..SPECIFY THE PERSON..) intending to destroy or damage property or being reckless as to whether property would be destroyed or damaged and intending by the

(E)_[destruction]_
(F)_[damage]_

to endanger the life of

(G)_[another]_
(H)_[ **(..SPECIFY THE PERSON ENDANGERED..)]_

or being reckless as to whether the life of another would be thereby endangered
english.legislation: Contrary to sections 1(2), 1(3) and 4 of the Criminal Damage Act 1971.

english.notes:
(i) This offence has been made obsolete and replaced with two separate offences - one where there is an intention to endanger life (see document H20247), and one where there is recklessness as to whether life was endangered (see document H20248).
(ii) With aggravated offence, recklessness as to whether life endangered must be charged separately - R v Hoof (1981).
(iii) The consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions is required where the damage is to a spouse's property (section 30(4) of the Theft Act 1968).
(iv) Property damaged or destroyed may belong to defendant.
(v) The same incident may involve separate activities, some causing ordinary damage and some damage by fire (for example, protestors break into a laboratory building, smash laboratory equipment and set fire to some files). In such circumstances they are separate offences and best charged as such (R v Booth 1999).
